entries.title: The Poor Little Old Lady
entries.author: Rafael Pombo
entries.sourceNote: AI-assisted English rendering; human review pending. The linked Spanish edition remains the canonical source.
stanzas:
Once there was a little old lady
with not a thing to eat
but meats, fruits, sweets,
cakes, eggs, bread, and fish.

She drank broth, chocolate,
milk, wine, tea, and coffee,
and the poor thing could not find
what to eat or what to drink.

And this old woman had not
even a little hut to live in
except a great big house
with its orchard and its garden.

No one, no one cared for her
except Andrés and Juan and Gil,
and eight servants and two pages
in livery and bow ties.

She never had a place to sit
but chairs and sofas,
with little stools and cushions
and springs in the backrests.

Nor any other bed than a great one,
more golden than an altar,
with a soft-feather mattress,
much silk and lots of ruffle.

And this poor little old lady,
each year, to the very end,
had one year more of age
and one year less to live.

And when she looked in the mirror,
she was always frightened to see there
another old woman in spectacles,
a cap and a toupee.

And this poor little old lady
had nothing to wear
but dresses of a thousand cuts
in a thousand kinds of cloth.

And if not for her shoes,
slippers, boots, and pumps,
barefoot across the floor
the poor woman would have gone.

She never had an appetite
once she had finished eating,
nor did she ever enjoy perfect health
whenever she was not feeling well.

She died of a sickness of wrinkles,
already bent like a three,
and never again complained
of hunger or of thirst.

And this poor little old lady,
when she died, left behind
nothing but ounces, jewels, lands, houses,
eight cats and a troupial.

Sleep in peace, and may God allow
us to manage to enjoy
the poverty of that poor old woman
and die of that very same disease.

entries.title: Simon the Simpleton
entries.author: Rafael Pombo
entries.sourceNote: AI-assisted English rendering; human review pending. The linked Spanish edition remains the canonical source.
stanzas:
Simon the Simpleton called the baker:
‘Let me see the cakes! I want to try them!’
‘Yes,’ replied the other, ‘but first I want to see
that coin with which you mean to pay.’
Good little Simon searched his pockets
and said: ‘Indeed! I don’t have a single one.’

Simon the Simpleton likes fish
and wants to become a fisherman too,
and spends the hours sitting, sitting,
fishing in Mama Leonor’s bucket.

Little Simon made a snow cake
and, hungry, threw it on the embers to bake,
but the little cake melted at once,
and put the embers out; he ate nothing.

Simon saw thistles carrying plums
and said: ‘How good! I’ll pick them.’
But worse than needles and rowel points
they made him jump and whistle and bite.

He washed with black shoe polish
because his mother gave him no soap,
and when the cats were hunting mice
he frightened the cat, shouting: ‘Mouse!’

One day, milking the spotted cow,
he squeezed her tail instead of the teat;
and—there goes the cow!—she kicked him so hard
that Don Simon spun like a top.

And he fell astride the heifer,
and the young cow got angry too,
and there was another jump and another kicking
and two tumbles in a heartbeat.

He mounted a donkey he found in the market
and set off merrily to hunt deer;
he flew through the streets without seeing a deer,
rolled over the stones, and the ass ran away.
Taita Lucio sent him to buy a loin,
and he brought it home with great care,
hanging it by the tail of a gray horse
so it would arrive clean and tasty.

Just as the ice was beginning to set,
Simon the Simpleton went skating,
when suddenly the ground broke beneath him
and he cried: ‘I’m drowning! Come pull me out!’

Climbing a tree to steal a nest,
the poor little home of a singing blackbird,
the branch broke; Simon let out a scream,
and he fell into a foul-smelling pit.

He saw a duck, took aim, and fired his blunderbuss;
returning home he said to his father:
‘Papa, I cannot kill a little bird
because when I shoot, it gets frightened and flies away.’

Seeing a saucer full of mustard,
he took a big swallow, thinking it was honey,
and raged and dribbled foam
with such a tongue and carnation-red eyes.

He saw a pile of earth blocking the road
and some people asking: ‘What shall we do here?’
‘Fools!’ said the boy, solving the matter;
‘dig a big hole and put it in there.’
They sent him for water, and he flew off
carrying a sieve to pour it into;
as soon as good little Simon brings it back,
his picturesque, faithful story will continue.

entries.title: Rin Rin the Tadpole
entries.author: Rafael Pombo
entries.sourceNote: AI-assisted English rendering; human review pending. The linked Spanish edition remains the canonical source.
stanzas:
The son of Frog, Rin Rin the Tadpole,
went out this morning, all stiff and smart,
in short trousers, a fashionable tie,
a ribboned hat and a wedding coat.
‘Boy, don’t go out!’ his mother cries,
but he makes a gesture and proudly goes.

On the way he met a neighbor mouse
and said: ‘Friend! Come with me,
let’s visit Mrs. Mouse together
and there will be revelry and a feast.’

Soon they arrived, and Mouse stepped forward,
stretched his neck, and took hold of the knocker.
He knocked two or three times; they asked: ‘Who is it?’
‘It is I, Mrs. Mouse; I kiss your feet.’

‘Are you home?’ —‘Yes, sir, yes, I am;
and I am delighted to see you both today.
I was at my work, spinning cotton,
but that does not matter: welcome!’

They bowed and shook hands,
and Ratico, who was more seasoned, said:
‘My green friend, I am burning with heat;
give him some beer, please.’

While the rascal drank the jug dry,
the lady ordered the guitar brought
and asked Little Tadpole to sing
cheerful verses, an elegant tune.
‘Oh, gladly I would, ma’am;
but I cannot please you now,
for my throat is drier than tow
and this new outfit is squeezing me.’

‘I am terribly sorry,’ Aunt Rat replied;
‘loosen your vest and tie a little,
and meanwhile I will sing you
a very particular little song.’

But while this brilliant party was underway
with dancing and beer, guitar and song,
the Cat and her Cats crossed the threshold,
and everything became a final judgment.
Old Mother Cat grabbed little Ratico by the ear, meowing: ‘Hello!’
and the kitten Cats grabbed old Mrs. Rat,
one by the paw and the other by the tail.
Don Tadpole, seeing this assault,
took his hat, made a tremendous leap,
and opening the door with hands and nose,
went off wishing everyone a very happy night.

And he kept leaping higher and faster,
lost his hat, tore his shirt,
slipped into the mouth of a greedy duck
and it gulped him down in one long swallow.
And so ended the tale, one, two, three:
Mouse and Mrs. Mouse, and Frog afterward;
the Cats ate, and the Duck had dinner,
and Mama Frog was left all alone!

entries.title: Mirringa Mirronga
entries.author: Rafael Pombo
entries.sourceNote: AI-assisted English rendering; human review pending. The linked Spanish edition remains the canonical source.
stanzas:
Mirringa Mirronga, the sly lady cat
is going to throw a party, playing hide-and-seek,
and wants all the tomcats and cats
to eat no mice for lunch or rats for dinner.

‘Let’s see my glasses, and pen and inkwell,
and let’s put the invitations down first.
Let Fuñas and Fanfarriñas come,
and Ñoño and Marroño and Tompo and his girls.’

‘Now let’s see what the pantry has.
There is chicken and fish—the thing is good!
And cakes and fowls and meat without fat.
What a kind lady, the lady of the house!’

‘Come, my little kitties Mirrín and Mirrón.
Fly to the room of Mama Hearth
for eight bowls and four trays
that are not cracked, nor broken, nor old.
Come, my little kitties Mirrón and Mirrín,
bring the basket and the dindirindín,
and off to market! We are short of lettuce
and turnips and cabbages and rice and turtle.’

‘Tell my little mistress I have guests,
that she should not come see me, lest she fall ill;
tomorrow itself I will return her dishes,
I thank her very much and they are very cheap.
Careful, little paws, if you muddy the floor!
Dust it, scrub it, sweep it—
the flowers, the table, the soup!... Ding-a-ling!
The people are arriving. Jesus, what a bustle!’

They arrived by carriage late at night,
gentlemen and ladies, with many bows,
in grand uniforms, tails and gloves,
with very stiff collars and elegant frock coats.

As Mirriña the one-eyed cat closed the door
she bit her tail in a somersault,
but smelled the bacon and said: ‘Miaow!’
‘This is a banquet fit for a king!’

With very good manners they all sat down,
had the soup and raised their glasses;
the fried fish was exquisite
and the boneless turkey a delight.

Mirringa Mirronga offers them everything:
‘Shall I serve you breast?’ —‘As you wish.’
‘And I will give you fish; it is delicate.’
‘If you fancy it, do not stand on ceremony:
have more without fear.’ And he says: ‘I agree.’
But alas! A thorny bone gets stuck in one man’s throat,
and beautiful Ñoña, who is skillful,
putting the bellows to him says: ‘Breathe!’

Mirriña the Cuca struck him on the nape
and at once the devilish splinter passed;
they served dessert and then coffee,
and the dance began with a minuet.

There were waltz, quadrilles, polka and mazurka,
and Tompo, who was with máxima turca,
got Ñoña’s dress tangled in his claws
and both fell to the floor, and she was undone.

All the dancers laughed like cats
and the revelry went on merrier than before,
and Mirringa shouted: ‘I have shut the door!
Until dawn, no one leaves!’
But what a misfortune! Doña Engracia entered
and made quite a serious cat-fight,
handing them Uncle Pegadizo’s sausage
so they could make suppers with other people’s cakes.

bio: Rafael Pombo (Bogotá, 1833–1912) was a poet, translator, and author of a wide-ranging body of work that includes poetry, fables, stories, and texts for children.
The comparison edition consulted describes a body of more than 1,400 poems and notes that the first edition of his complete works appeared in 1916 in four volumes.

entries.title: The Bandit Cat
entries.author: Rafael Pombo
entries.sourceNote: AI-assisted English rendering; human review pending. The linked Spanish edition remains the canonical source.
stanzas:
Michín said to his mother:
‘I am going to turn into Pateta,
and whoever tries to stop me
will die on the spot.
I have already stolen Dad’s
dagger and pistols; now I am
armed and ready, and I am going
to rob and kill people,
and never again—remember this!—
will you see Michín from today.’

Going into the woods, he met
a rooster on the road,
and said: ‘Let’s see how good my aim
is for killing.’
Standing ready, he fired;
the mountain thundered at the shot.
Michín bruised a toe
and singed his mustache;
but with its neck shot through,
the rooster fell flat.

Then he climbed to steal,
tempted by his hunger,
an owl’s nest,
which flared into fury upon seeing him;
but the branch broke,
hat and dagger went flying,
and to an infernal whistle
that drilled his ears
the criminal fugitive fell,
spinning and howling.

Recovered from his fall,
he saw another cat and attacked.
‘Namesake, stop right there!
Your purse or your life!’
The other was not intimidated
and instead shouted: ‘Stop, thief!’
The rascal fired; the gun exploded
at the breech,
and Michín was nearly smashed
by the impact.

Another day, meeting
a great bandit dog,
the sly one approached him
with kindness and courtesy:
‘Comrade,’ he said,
‘let’s celebrate our alliance.’
And so they did: jokes,
dancing and brandy, until at last
Michín fell exhausted
and scratched his belly.

‘Comrade,’ said the dog,
‘we must pool our riches
and secure the money
by burying it.’
There was an error in the counting
and a shout and quarrel broke out,
until the dog took up
the club with both hands:
it whizzed, he fell, and his pal
lay half dead.

With the cool morning air
Michín regained consciousness
and found himself one-armed, crippled,
blind in one eye, hungry and penniless.
Meanwhile his rival
went barking with laughter,
ears drooping
and tail between his legs,
while Michín wept in tender voices
over all his misdeeds.

He picked up his little hat,
and under a scorching sun
step by step he went home
with a humble, contrite air.
‘I confess my great crime,
and I must atone for it,’
he said to his mother; ‘you will see
I will never be bad again.
Oh, Mommy, give me a beating—
but give me something to eat!’
